is facing major travel disruptions as Typhoon Saudel, also known as Typhoon No. 18, sweeps across the Okinawa region with powerful winds, torrential rain and dangerous seas. The storm struck at a particularly difficult time, arriving just as Japan’s summer holiday travel period was coming to an end and thousands of people were preparing to return home.

According to the latest information, 279 domestic and international flights have been cancelled, directly affecting approximately 41,688 passengers. Japan’s major airlines, including ANA and Japan Airlines (JAL), were among those hit hardest. ANA cancelled all flights to and from Naha Airport in Okinawa on August 26, creating widespread disruption for travelers.

The storm’s impact has also reached international aviation. Regional carriers including Scoot, Tigerair and China Airlines have cancelled or adjusted services connecting Okinawa with destinations such as Taiwan and Singapore. Some flights have been forced to depart earlier, while others were cancelled altogether as airlines placed passenger safety ahead of schedules.

It is not only the skies that have been affected. Ferry services connecting Okinawa with surrounding islands have also been suspended because of extremely rough seas. For island communities and travelers relying on marine transportation, the storm has created another major obstacle to movement.

The Japan Meteorological Agency has warned of dangerous conditions as the typhoon carries extremely powerful winds. Peak instantaneous gusts have reportedly reached around 234 kilometers per hour, equivalent to approximately 65 meters per second. The storm’s central atmospheric pressure has fallen to around 950 hectopascals, highlighting its significant strength.

Authorities are warning residents about the possibility of destructive winds, torrential rainfall, storm surges and landslides. Waves around Okinawa could reach extraordinary heights, with forecasts warning of waves of up to approximately 9 meters in affected waters. Power outages have already begun affecting parts of northern Okinawa.

Typhoon Saudel is moving west-northwest at approximately 20 kilometers per hour, passing the Okinawa main island and the Amami Islands of Kagoshima Prefecture. After moving through the Ryukyu island chain, the storm is expected to continue westward across the East China Sea.

Forecasts indicate that Saudel could approach the southeastern coast of China’s Fujian Province around late August 27 or early August 28, although the exact track and intensity can still change.

With the storm threatening communities, transportation and infrastructure, Japanese authorities are urging residents to remain vigilant, monitor official evacuation information and take action before conditions become dangerous.

The storm has also prompted precautions involving the U.S. military presence in Okinawa. Ships and aircraft have reportedly been moved away from the typhoon’s projected path to reduce the risk of damage as the storm’s expanding wind field approaches major military facilities, including the area around Kadena Air Base.

is facing major travel disruptions as Typhoon Saudel, also known as Typhoon No. 18, sweeps across the Okinawa region with powerful winds, torrential rain and dangerous seas. The storm struck at a particularly difficult time, arriving just as Japan’s summer holiday travel period was coming to an end and thousands of people were preparing to return home.

According to the latest information, 279 domestic and international flights have been cancelled, directly affecting approximately 41,688 passengers. Japan’s major airlines, including ANA and Japan Airlines (JAL), were among those hit hardest. ANA cancelled all flights to and from Naha Airport in Okinawa on August 26, creating widespread disruption for travelers.

The storm’s impact has also reached international aviation. Regional carriers including Scoot, Tigerair and China Airlines have cancelled or adjusted services connecting Okinawa with destinations such as Taiwan and Singapore. Some flights have been forced to depart earlier, while others were cancelled altogether as airlines placed passenger safety ahead of schedules.

It is not only the skies that have been affected. Ferry services connecting Okinawa with surrounding islands have also been suspended because of extremely rough seas. For island communities and travelers relying on marine transportation, the storm has created another major obstacle to movement.

The Japan Meteorological Agency has warned of dangerous conditions as the typhoon carries extremely powerful winds. Peak instantaneous gusts have reportedly reached around 234 kilometers per hour, equivalent to approximately 65 meters per second. The storm’s central atmospheric pressure has fallen to around 950 hectopascals, highlighting its significant strength.

Authorities are warning residents about the possibility of destructive winds, torrential rainfall, storm surges and landslides. Waves around Okinawa could reach extraordinary heights, with forecasts warning of waves of up to approximately 9 meters in affected waters. Power outages have already begun affecting parts of northern Okinawa.

Typhoon Saudel is moving west-northwest at approximately 20 kilometers per hour, passing the Okinawa main island and the Amami Islands of Kagoshima Prefecture. After moving through the Ryukyu island chain, the storm is expected to continue westward across the East China Sea.

Forecasts indicate that Saudel could approach the southeastern coast of China’s Fujian Province around late August 27 or early August 28, although the exact track and intensity can still change.

With the storm threatening communities, transportation and infrastructure, Japanese authorities are urging residents to remain vigilant, monitor official evacuation information and take action before conditions become dangerous.

The storm has also prompted precautions involving the U.S. military presence in Okinawa. Ships and aircraft have reportedly been moved away from the typhoon’s projected path to reduce the risk of damage as the storm’s expanding wind field approaches major military facilities, including the area around Kadena Air Base.

So has been with my gf for a couple of years and she has been complaining in front of me about my parents poor financial planning, resulting in not able to sponsor wedding or flat but I just comfort her every time and she has also accept the fact.

So one fine day, we were sharing with my family about our financial planning and some miscommunication occurred and my gf, in the heat of the convo, tell my parents she doesn’t want to be like them to be poor after working their whole life… my parents handled it really well and stop the convo and went out for their dinner.

I think it’s fine if we complain in front of me but to say in front of my parents, I think that’s a little rude to be doing to the elderly generation.
